item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] What's driving the rising unrest in Pakistan-administered Kashmir?
item.description:
What's driving the rising unrest in Pakistan-administered Kashmir? 

Submitted by MEE correspondent on Tue, 08/04/2026 - 18:36
Frustration over basic affordability has mushroomed into a broader critique of the region's governance
Protesters burn tyres along a road after clashes with police in Muzaffarabad amid unrest during the first phase of voting for the local legislature in Pakistan-administered Kashmir, on 31 July 2026 (Sajjad Qayyum/AFP)
Off

For decades, global attention on Kashmir has focused overwhelmingly on the Indian-administered side of the Line of Control (LoC), the heavily militarised de facto border that divides the disputed Himalayan region between India and Pakistan. 

International headlines have largely revolved around repression, insurgency, military deployments, and diplomatic confrontation. 

Far less attention has been paid to the political currents unfolding across the LoC in Pakistan-administered Kashmir, officially known as Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK). 

Long portrayed by Islamabad as a model of self-governance in contrast to Indian-administered Kashmir, the territory is now witnessing some of the most significant popular unrest in recent decades. 

What started as frustration over soaring electricity bills and flour prices has rapidly transformed into a systemic challenge to Islamabad’s authority in the region. Rather than rehashing the old geopolitical tug-of-war with India, this new wave of unrest reflects deep-seated frustration with local governance. 

Protesters are demanding genuine political participation, arguing that while Kashmir’s international fate hangs in limbo, their basic political and economic rights cannot remain frozen. In a region long treated as a geopolitical pawn, domestic disillusionment is now taking centre stage. 

From economic grievances to political awakening 

The protests have been led by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a loose coalition of traders, lawyers, students, civil society activists, and local political figures that emerged in 2023 outside the traditional party structure. 

Rejecting established Pakistani political parties as ineffective or overly dependent on Islamabad, the JAAC focused directly on basic issues: high electricity bills, rising flour prices, heavy taxation, and poor public services. 

'What we need to know is who will provide us with jobs and a fair life today'

- Mujtaba Naqvi, JAAC supporter

This message quickly united a region facing serious economic hardship. 

Youth unemployment in the area sits at roughly 27 percent, nearly triple Pakistan’s national average, while fewer than eight percent of women are in the formal workforce, Danish Khan, co-director of ‘The Inequality, Poverty, Power and Social Justice Initiative’ at Franklin & Marshall College, recently wrote in a piece for The Friday Times.

As he noted, the region was generating a growing “reserve army of young unemployed people”.

Development in the mountainous region continues to lag behind the rest of the country. Substandard roads severely restrict access to essential public services like healthcare and education, a situation that becomes especially dire during its harsh winters. 

Meanwhile, many communities still bear the visible scars and lingering devastation of the 2005 earthquake that killed tens of thousands of people. 

What began as a fight for affordable living soon sparked massive demonstrations across major towns, shutting down markets and forcing officials to negotiate. By 2024 and 2025, the government yielded to key demands: lowering electricity rates and subsidising wheat compared to the rest of the country. 

But many activists view these concessions as temporary quick fixes.

“The price reductions addressed immediate grievances,” says political economy researcher Faisal Mir, “but they did not address the deeper structures of economic exclusion.” 

The campaign against inflation has now mushroomed into a broader critique of governance, linking daily hardship directly to political arrangements that concentrate power away from the region. 

A younger generation, weary of traditional rhetoric about competing nationalisms, is now demanding accountability, transparency, and genuine representation. Rather than debating Kashmir’s future status, they are asking who governs them today and whose interests those leaders truly serve. 

“No one knows when the Kashmir dispute will finally be resolved,” Mujtaba Naqvi, a JAAC supporter in the regional capital of Muzaffarabad, told Middle East Eye. “What we need to know is who will provide us with jobs and a fair life today.”

Battle over refugee representation

These questions have led directly to one of the most contentious features of Pakistan-administered Kashmir’s constitutional framework: the legislative seats reserved for Kashmiri refugees living outside the territory. 

'Erasing historical facts': India orders massive crackdown on books in Kashmir's libraries
Read More »

On paper, AJK, with a population of around five million, functions under a semi-autonomous structure complete with its own president, prime minister, parliament, and supreme court. Candidates must swear allegiance to Pakistan to run for office.

The core of the current disputes lies in how the assembly is structured. 

Out of 53 total seats, 33 are elected by residents living inside the territory. The remaining 12 are reserved for Kashmiris who migrated to Pakistan from Indian-administered Kashmir during and after the 1947 and 1965 wars. Although these voters reside across Pakistan’s four provinces rather than in AJK, they continue to elect representatives to the regional assembly. 

Supporters maintain that these 12 seats safeguard the political rights of displaced families and uphold Islamabad’s diplomatic argument that the entire former princely state remains disputed internationally. 

Stripping refugee representation, they contend, would weaken Pakistan's position in a high-stakes standoff with India - a conflict that has triggered multiple wars since British India's partition in 1947, as well as a brief four-day military confrontation last year. 

The region’s supreme court in early June ruled that the 12 refugee seats are constitutionally protected. 

However, the JAAC and other local critics view the arrangement as a backdoor for federal meddling. Federal parties frequently use these 12 constituencies to swing majorities in Muzaffarabad. This setup has fuelled acute political turbulence, leaving AJK with four different prime ministers in the current regional assembly in rapid succession.

“These 12 seats continuously dictate government formation,” political activist Raja Nafees, who supports JAAC's demands, told MEE. “Voters who don't even live here end up deciding who rules us.”

A crisis of legitimacy

For decades, mainstream political parties in AJK, acting largely as extensions of Islamabad, dominated regional politics unchallenged. Today, that status quo has shattered.

Unsettled by widespread unrest and informal boycott calls led by the JAAC over the 12 reserved refugee seats, authorities staggered the regional elections across three phases between 27 July and 10 August. 

The strategy backfired: voter turnout plummeted during the first two phases, leading analysts to declare the election null and void, and warning that the resulting assembly will lack a credible mandate. 

Political infighting has further eroded trust, with the Pakistan People’s Party, led by President Asif Ali Zardari, accusing the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif of rigging the polls. 

At the same time, the nationalist slogan “Kashmir Banega Khudmukhtar” (Kashmir will be sovereign), promoted by groups like the Jammu Kashmir Liberation Front (JKLF), has gained unprecedented public traction in the protests. This reflects an emerging political vocabulary that moves beyond the traditional choice between India and Pakistan. 

Negotiation, crackdown and uncertainty

Since protests flared up in 2024, authorities in Islamabad and Muzaffarabad have tackled the uprising using a volatile mix of concessions and coercion. 

While early negotiations yielded subsidies on electricity and flour, the government adopted a harsher stance as demonstrations expanded into demands for structural political reform.

When the JAAC announced a protest march from Rawalakot to Muzaffarabad on 9 June, Pakistani authorities accused the group of disrupting public order. On 5 June, the movement was banned under anti-terrorism laws, and key leaders, including JAAC leader Shaukat Mir, were arrested. 

After negotiations failed again on 26 July, the JAAC called for a renewed march. However, the group accused state forces of using lethal violence to stop protesters. 

Independent estimates indicate over 45 people, primarily protesters, alongside law enforcement personnel and bystanders, have been killed in clashes since 5 June. 

Official details remain scarce as widespread internet blackouts and strict curfews severely hinder independent verification. 

Government officials maintain that constitutional disputes should be handled through legal avenues rather than through street protest. 

In a press briefing on 31 July, military spokesperson Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry stated that the region has historically received state attention, care, and resource allocation.

He said that authorities had “wholeheartedly” urged the JAAC to contest elections and pursue reform through courts and parliament. 

“But they want to pursue this by force, but only the state has the monopoly of violence," he added. 

Other government ministers went further, dismissing the JAAC as an “armed mob” and levelling unfounded accusations that the group had ties to India and Taliban militants. 

JAAC leadership firmly denies these claims, maintaining that their campaign remains peaceful and rooted in basic democratic rights. 

Amid the standoff, locals are bearing the brunt of the consequences. Continuous internet network blackouts have crippled daily commerce and tourism. In Rawalakot, the movement’s stronghold, where leaders called for a mass march, heavy curfews and road blockades brought the peak summer season to a halt.

Local traders face mounting financial ruin, while residents endure severe communication outages and disrupted basic services, leaving the region locked in deep uncertainty. 

Fallout from Article 370 in India

The constitutional debate in AJK has also unfolded against the backdrop of India's August 2019 revocation of Article 370. 

After ‘testing ground’ in Kashmir, pellet guns used on student protesters in India's capital
Read More »

By ending the limited autonomy and erstwhile "special status" of Indian-administered Kashmir and placing it under direct federal control, New Delhi fundamentally transformed the political landscape across both sides of the LoC. 

The move sparked widespread criticism from Pakistan and ignited major local demonstrations. When protesters, organised by groups like the JKLF, attempted to march toward the LoC in solidarity, Pakistani authorities forcibly stopped them. Analysts note that key organisers of those marches now help lead the JAAC. 

Perceiving Islamabad’s diplomatic response as inadequate, many AJK residents began questioning Pakistan’s commitment to preserving their distinct identity. 

Crucially, the region’s unresolved status complicates major infrastructure investments, particularly under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor. This has fuelled widespread speculation that Islamabad might eventually redefine AJK's legal status, potentially merging it with neighbouring Pakistani districts or converting it into a province. 

Although the government has never voiced those ambitions, this pervasive anxiety has reshaped public discourse, deepening institutional distrust and strongly reinforcing local demands for greater regional autonomy.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] 'Collective punishment': US Supreme Court greenlights $656m judgement against Palestinian officials
item.description:
'Collective punishment': US Supreme Court greenlights $656m judgement against Palestinian officials

Submitted by MEE staff on Tue, 08/04/2026 - 19:00
The case was brought by US victims of attacks in Israel some 25 years ago
A young Palestinian man walks past destroyed cars, burned by Israeli settlers overnight, in Jalud, near Nablus, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on 4 August 2026 (Mohammed Torokman/Reuters)
Off

The US Supreme Court has refused to freeze a $656m judgement against the Palestinian Authority (PA) and the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) after the two groups said they were too cash-strapped to compensate Americans for attacks in Israel during the Second Intifada.

The decision was announced on Monday by Justice Sonia Sotomayor, a liberal justice who is tasked with taking on emergency case reviews.

This comes 22 years after the lawsuit was first launched, and it means the collection of the funds can begin immediately.

In 2015, the plaintiffs, who said they were victims of attacks between 2002 and 2004, won the damages.

Then in 2016, the US Circuit Court of Appeals tossed out the judgment on the grounds that US courts cannot consider lawsuits against foreign groups if the violence was not aimed at American citizens. 

Last year, the supreme court revived the case by voting 9-0 to uphold the Promoting Security and Justice for Victims of Terrorism Act passed by lawmakers.

By March of this year, the US Circuit Court of Appeals reinstated the judgment. 

"Congress passed special laws to make the Palestinian Authority submit to US jurisdiction against its will if it continued to provide families of martyred Palestinians with salaries," Raed Jarrar, advocacy director with Democracy for the Arab World Now (Dawn), told Middle East Eye.

The PA, he added, was "forced into accepting US jurisdiction [and it's] really unprecedented". 

The PA and PLO have said that a $656m payout would destabilise their governing abilities in the occupied West Bank, where Israel has long withheld Palestinian tax revenue from the PA.

"The judgment will affect ordinary Palestinians who are already operating on a 70 percent salary because the PA is a dysfunctional and for-profit institution that is unable to even pay the full salaries of its employees," Jarrar explained.

"It will be levied against doctors and engineers and government employees. It is the closest we can get to an act of collective punishment... these are ordinary Palestinians."

The uprisings

The PA is the governing body that has overseen areas of the occupied West Bank since 1994, as part of the Oslo Accords peace agreement between Israel and the PLO.

The PLO is an umbrella political coalition that is internationally recognised as the official representative of the Palestinian people in both the Palestinian territories and the diaspora.

The Second Intifada, or uprising, began on 28 September 2000, when then-Israeli opposition leader, the vehemently right-wing Ariel Sharon, led a delegation to the Al-Aqsa complex, in what was seen by Palestinians as an act of provocation.

When mass rallies broke out in response, the Israeli army responded with deadly violence, killing nearly 50 Palestinians in the first five days.

The Second Intifada is largely remembered for Israel's killing of 12-year-old Palestinian Mohammed al-Durrah as news cameras were rolling, in what became the first instance of a live-streamed shooting of a child hiding behind his father. The father survived. 

Mohammed became a symbol of the Palestinian struggle against the occupation. 

The Second Intifada lasted some five years, with Israeli forces killing nearly 5,000 Palestinians. 

A thousand Israelis were killed in bombings and attacks carried out by Palestinians inside Israel. 

Separate rules

Monday's supreme court decision brings into sharp focus the notion that foreign governments and leaders can face legal repercussions in the US, while the US repudiates and undermines the international courts that were specifically designed to bring accountability to victims of mass murder.

In July 2025, the US said it was placing sanctions on officials in the PA and PLO over their work taking Israel to those courts.

According to the State Department, the unnamed officials were “not complying with their commitments and undermining the prospects for peace”.

It cited “initiating and supporting actions at international organizations” and “taking actions to internationalize its conflict with Israel such as through the International Criminal Court (ICC) and International Court of Justice (ICJ)”.

Washington accused the figures of violating the PLO Commitments Compliance Act of 1989 (PLOCCA) and the Middle East Peace Commitments Act of 2002 (MEPCA).

Since the Israeli assault on Gaza began in October 2023, killing more than 74,000 Palestinians, Israel has found itself diplomatically isolated.

This has been furthered by deadly Israeli settler attacks in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem.

In September 2025, the Trump administration announced it would revoke and deny visas to anyone affiliated with the PLO and PA, and demanded the groups "consistently repudiate terrorism”, citing the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks on southern Israel, according to a US State Department press release.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Saudi Aramco reports bumper profits as it bypasses Strait of Hormuz
item.description:
Saudi Aramco reports bumper profits as it bypasses Strait of Hormuz

Submitted by Sean Mathews on Tue, 08/04/2026 - 21:09
The East-West Pipeline has been a model for states from the UAE to Syria looking to get around Iran's leverage on the waterway
Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser speaks during the annual Future Investment Initiative conference in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on 29 October 2024 (Fayez Nureldine/AFP)
Off

Saudi Aramco said on Tuesday its profits surged 33 percent in the second quarter of this year, as the kingdom benefited from the US-Israeli war on Iran, which drove up energy prices, while its oil pipeline allowed it to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.

The state-owned Saudi Arabian oil giant’s adjusted net income rose to $33.4bn from $25.2bn a year ago. The second quarter runs from early April to the end of June. The US and Iran reached a ceasefire in April that was extended in June, but fighting has continued to rage, keeping energy prices inflated.

Iran is attempting to assert its control over the Strait of Hormuz and has attacked dozens of vessels trying to transit the strait via Oman’s territorial waters. The US has bombarded Iran, and in response, Tehran has targeted Gulf states, particularly Kuwait and Bahrain.

The war drove Brent, the international benchmark, up above $100 per barrel in May and then again in July. Prices for refined products, like diesel, jet fuel, and gasoline, are up substantially.

Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain, and Qatar have all had to cancel or massively curb energy shipments.

However, Saudi Arabia has been able to export around two-thirds of its pre-war oil capacity because of the East-West Pipeline, which connects the kingdom’s eastern oil fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu.

Aramco CEO Amin Nasser noted the pipeline’s importance to the company while commenting on the results, according to a press statement.   

“Despite the unprecedented supply disruption through the Strait of Hormuz, we continued to demonstrate our ability to maintain business continuity by capitalising on our diverse asset base and multi-decade planning, including strategic infrastructure such as the East-West Pipeline, storage capacity, and export terminals,” he said.

A model

The East-West Pipeline has become a model for other Middle Eastern states looking to bypass the Strait of Hormuz in the coming years. Experts told Middle East Eye that tens of billions of dollars will be spent on new infrastructure in the coming years to get around Hormuz.

From Syria to UAE, the race to bypass Strait of Hormuz is on
Read More »

“When we speak to our customers in the region, they say they never want to deal with this again,” Artem Abramov, the deputy head of analysis at Rystad Energy, previously told MEE. “These bypass projects will move forward.”

The UAE is building a second pipeline to the port of Fujairah to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, doubling its export capacity by 2027.

Meanwhile, Iraq - the second-largest producer in the oil cartel Opec - signed a deal with Syria in July to rehabilitate a pipeline from its northern oil fields to Syria’s Mediterranean coast. MEE was the first to reveal the project and its US backing.

Aramco is not the only energy company that has benefited from the war. ExxonMobil and Chevron, the US’s energy behemoths, reported sky-high earnings in the second quarter also.

ExxonMobil’s profits doubled from a year earlier while Chevron had its highest quarterly earnings on record.

Trump, who is grappling with an unpopular war and frustration over high gasoline prices, has singled out the companies.

“Chevron: too much money. ExxonMobil: too much money,” Trump said. “They’re going to give some of that back to the public and they better cut the retail price, the consumer price,” he told reporters on Monday.

Brent has dropped about eight percent to $79 per barrel since Sunday, after Trump retreated from his threat to unleash the "biggest" bombing campaign since WWII on Iran.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday that the US and Iran were close to a deal to stop fighting and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] US depleted 'virtually all' long-range precision missiles during Iran war: Report
item.description:
US depleted 'virtually all' long-range precision missiles during Iran war: Report

The US has exhausted its stockpile of sophisticated long-range missiles during the war on Iran, suggesting that there are supply limits to President Donald Trump’s threat to subject the Islamic Republic to the "biggest attack" since World War II.

The US has drained its supply of surface-to-surface weapons, known as Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM), Reuters reported on Tuesday, citing two sources who said the US had used "virtually all" of these munitions.

These long-range missiles are a critical part of the US’s arsenal, allowing it to accurately target foes from a distance without relying on warplanes that are vulnerable to air defence systems.

Reuters reported that US Central Command - which oversees military operations in the Middle East - has had to replenish its stock of surface-to-surface missiles from other theatres of operation.
